How Premier League's massive six keep getting richer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.
  • Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.
  • In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

And the gap is growing. Every season.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the massive six have exploded, examines fresh trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

Industry observers note that companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance concerns.

Let's look at how the gap has grown.

We will use Everton, the only club not in the major six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

Sources indicate that in 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was Â£120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to Â£442m.

So what has driven this huge escalation?

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The substantial football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire remarked.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices.".

Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.

In a recent development, it means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League strategy was torpedoed, Uefa created a newly introduced financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or Â£713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned Â£37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool Â£35.5m and Chelsea Â£33.3m. Newcastle received only Â£13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Their value pillar is projected to be worth Â£25m this season. But that will still be less than the significant six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the substantial six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.

Not just by a small amount. They were Â£74m behind Tottenham, and Â£200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.

City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.

City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.

The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.

Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.

Sources indicate that stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the massive six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of Â£80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their major six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

Industry observers note that "Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire stated. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast.".

According to recent reports, matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only Â£16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by Â£69m and Spurs, thanks to their fresh ground, by Â£85m.

Recent findings suggest that "Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

It has been revealed that "Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial.".

Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire stated. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.

Recent findings suggest that "SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't.".

It has been revealed that the significant six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the massive six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire noted.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues.".

Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent Â£3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the Â£3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire stated.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under Â£100m.".

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

And you can see why it is concerned.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than Â£40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the significant six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an key point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the massive six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the massive six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the substantial-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire mentioned.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are Â£60m and Â£70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years.".

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the significant six.

The commercial power of the significant six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending Â£945m on players in the past five years.

The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the massive six and the rest.

Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.
  • In a recent development, presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday.
  • At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

In a recent development, presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that the 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Sources indicate that second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin.".

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she noted.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

It has been revealed that the prize winner also remarked she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

It has been revealed that in his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he noted, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

In a recent development, "I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he noted.

In a recent development, the jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set latest standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue.".

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from.".

#25286. ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1176 w)
📖 Baca

‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of latest research and guidelines for pregnant players.
  • Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.
  • It has been revealed that emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of latest research and guidelines for pregnant players.

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

It has been revealed that emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright unveiled her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

“I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” indicates 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”.

For many years, says the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa rolled out its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

According to recent reports, “I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” says Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

It has been revealed that “Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”.

Up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she claims. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

According to recent reports, “There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour notes. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”.

According to recent reports, some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she says. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”.

Sources indicate that though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

According to recent reports, but for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie says candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”.

Industry observers note that the other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she notes bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

Even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an key fact.

#25280. Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (994 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers.
  • Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager?
  • According to recent reports, although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers.

Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S.

According to recent reports, although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling.

Recent findings suggest that the United States’ interest in Pep Guardiola, and his talks with Italy earlier, have me wondering – what separates club and international management? Could Pep, as successful as he’s been, do well in either? – Joe P.

In a recent development, international and club management seem to me related but essentially different jobs. It’s one thing to have the players every day and be able to drill them over and over to impose a philosophy; quite another to pick them up for perhaps a dozen training sessions over a calendar year, plus major tournaments. International football is necessarily less sophisticated than club football, more based on individual excellence or heroism. Guardiola, you suspect, would be able to adapt, but it’s not certain. Plus there’s the fact that at major tournaments players are with their manager for a month or more, cooped up in the same hotel with no release. With the more intense coaches, such as Marcelo Bielsa, that seems to become problematic. And it’s notable that at the last World Cup the nations with the substantial-name managers – England, Brazil, the United States, Germany – fared less well than those who had appointed technocrats from within.

According to recent reports, michael Carrick’s firing highlighted the lack of top-class English managers. Why has an Englishman never managed a Premier League club to a title? – Ricky M.

According to recent reports, I think there are two related complications here. Are there any good English coaches? To which the answer appears to be that there are nowhere near as many as there ought to be. The various changes in player development enacted by the elite player performance proposal and the England DNA project have, over the past 10-15 years, led to the development of far more technically proficient English players than there have ever been before, which has been reflected in the uptick in England’s performances at major tournaments. St George’s Park was supposed to be about developing coaches as well as players but, as yet, that seems not to have happened.

That stated, it’s probably also the case that it’s very hard for British coaches to be appointed to top Premier League jobs. Say they get their start at a mid-sized Championship club and win promotion; they then have to amend their approach in the Premier League to scrap for points in a relegation battle. If they fail they are written off as not good enough for the top division; if they succeed, they’re seen as not playing the right sort of football for an elite club. It’s happened to Scott Parker … even the likes of Gary O’Neil or Eddie Howe seem somehow not quite right for the elite who, perhaps understandably, prefer to turn to somebody with experience of European competition.

Is there any part of you that feels sympathy for the current Man City players, who will presumably have to play out a “lost season” thanks to actions they had nothing to do with, and which probably happened long before their time at the club? – Jason D.

According to recent reports, to an extent, yes, but they’re pretty naïve if they didn’t realise the potential glitch they were walking into. I have far more sympathy for those players who played for clubs who were denied success by City’s cheating. It’s not just the teams who finished second in the league, lost to City in cup competitions or missed out on European qualification because of City; it’s those teams, most obviously Arsenal and Aston Villa, whose development was derailed by City taking their best players, offering wages and transfer fees that it turns out they had no business offering.

It has been revealed that italy have gotten some big results in the Nations League. Are they back? – Nicholas A.

Recent findings suggest that this question, to be fair, was sent in before the 4-1 defeat to Belgium on Sunday. But anyway, beating France at home may be a big result, but that and two wins over Turkey seems limited evidence to say they’re back. They have definitely looked sharper under Roberto Mancini than they have probably since winning the Euros under him five years ago, but that’s a long way from being back. Even if they were to win the Euros in 2028, it wouldn’t alter the fact they haven’t qualified for three World Cups in a row. They need to qualify for 2030 and then probably get to at least the quarter-finals before you can start to say they may be back. And even then, Serie A is way off what it was at its peak – and how many of this squad would get in a Spain or England squad? Even being generous, probably no more than four or five.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United have hired Mauricio Pochettino – and his first transfer demand may break Arsenal hearts.

With the Red Devils languishing in the relegation zone after just three wins in all competitions this season, the Argentine knows that he needs to turn things around promptly, with January eyed as an opportunity to do business.

And Pochettino could well annoy former team-mate Mikel Arteta with a move he's requested from his bosses at Manchester United.

Pochettino and Arteta know each other well from playing together at Paris Saint-Germain, while the Basque was invited to become a member of Pochettino's staff during his time on the other side of North London, at Tottenham Hotspur.

It's perhaps no surprise then, given their similar outlook on the game, that the latest United boss has earmarked a long-time Arsenal target as his first signing in the Old Trafford dugout.

Fichajes in Spain have reported that Pochettino has requested the signing of Julian Alvarez after walking through the door at Carrington, with the Gunners well-known admirers.

Arteta spent much of the summer looking to convince the Atletico Madrid man to return to English football and sign for the Premier League champions – with Alvarez himself waiting up until deadline day for a move to Barcelona that never materialised.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The relationship between the Atleti man and their idol hasn't been the same since, and with Barça having moved on from the player and Raphinha thriving in the No.9 role, it appears the pathway to a Camp Nou move is closed.

If Alvarez still wants to leave the Metropolitano, Arsenal would be the sensible destination given their interest and the fact they didn't upgrade either on the left wing or up front over the summer – but interest from United would complicate matters, with Pochettino perhaps able to convince his compatriot he could build around him.

Alvarez was a huge hit during his time in the Premier League, though adored on the blue side of Manchester, where he won a Treble and a World Cup in his first full season as a Manchester City player.

The 26-year-old has continued to flourish under Diego Simeone, scoring 29 goals in all competitions in his first season and 20 the following campaign.

FourFourTwo understands that the finances may not be there for a January move, though with United, nothing should be ruled out.

Alvarez is worth €110 million, according to Transfermarkt. Manchester United face Liverpool when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya is the subject of interest from La Liga – with a new contract on the table.

The 31-year-old has established himself as arguably England's best goalkeeper since moving to North London, winning the Golden Glove in every season since he's been at Arsenal.

But with a contract expiring in 2028 and recent comments about his desire to move back to his native Spain, Raya's future has become a worry for Gooners, who don't want to lose a player who fixed a problem position for manager Mikel Arteta.

Last month, Sport Witness relayed comments that Raya made to Spanish outlet Marca about his desire to play in La Liga, following rumours that Real Madrid have shortlisted the Arsenal man as a potential replacement for Thibaut Courtois, who is a free agent from next summer.

Raya moved to Blackburn Rovers as a teenager and spent a year on loan in the English non-league – so has never experienced his native league, telling the publication, “Perhaps, in the future, I could play for a Spanish club: I’m Spanish, and naturally, I’d love to play there.”.

Despite the interest, and Raya recently turning 31 – making him the second-oldest player in Arteta's squad behind fellow custodian, Kepa Arrizabalaga – Sport Witness have now relayed a report from ESPN regarding the contract situation of four players at London Colney.

Both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice are expected to renew beyond 2028, while Piero Hincapie – who only joined permanently over the summer – is noted to be close to an extension, too.

Raya is listed, too, as a star “very close” to agreeing a new deal, which will likely reflect his status as one of the best in English football and highlight his importance to Arteta's football.

The Spaniard joined from Brentford in 2023, initially on loan, to the confusion of some fans who felt that then-keeper Aaron Ramsdale didn't need replacing, but Raya won over doubters with excellent reflex saves, superb cross-claiming and world-class distribution.

FourFourTwo understands that Gunners goalkeeping coach Inaki Cana was pivotal to the decision to sign his protege, with the pair having worked together previously, and Arsenal knocked back in their efforts to sign Raya while he was still in the Championship.

Despite being the second choice for La Roja behind Unai Simon, Raya won the World Cup with Spain over the summer along with club-mates Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi, off the back of keeping 19 clean sheets in Arsenal's first title-winning campaign in 22 years.

The stopper also reached the Champions League final, conceding just five goals en route to Budapest in 14 appearances.

It has been revealed that raya is worth €30 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal face Newcastle United when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations.
  • It has been revealed that I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006.
  • According to recent reports, as it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations.

It has been revealed that I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group.

According to recent reports, as it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it.

We felt unwelcome from the moment we arrived and we were not the only team to experience this. Nigeria exploited all avenues to play mind games with their opposition and to make them lose focus on the matches.

According to recent reports, we arrived early in the morning at the Murtala Muhammed international airport in Lagos and faced our first test: how to retrieve our luggage. Only one carousel was working, which meant we had to wait a long time for our bags to arrive. We had a training session planned for later in the day and were all eager to get to the hotel, settle in and prepare for our first practice.

In a recent development, as we stepped out the airport doors, we looked for the bus that was to take us there, but we didn’t see one anywhere. As players, we were irritable and impatient, and starting to show it. Some of us were slumped on our bags, others had taken up residence on the pavement, and we were all cranky, especially as it took over an hour before a bus arrived.

Like in Mozambique a few years before, the bus was too small. Another 21-seater and we were 27 – 20 players and seven support staff, as well as all our luggage. Luckily, most of us had experience of how to squeeze in and so we knew the drill. We also had the advantage of our bags travelling in a smaller vehicle behind the bus, so the only challenge was fitting all the bodies in.

Recent findings suggest that generally, we saw the lighter side of these things and laughed as some of us got comfortable on the floor and others had to make do with a teammate’s lap. But we lost our sense of humour when we realised we had no air-conditioning and the drive was going to last at least another hour. Some grumbling ensued, but we knew better than to complain at such an early stage, and it seemed that things would get better soon.

Sources indicate that when we got to the hotel, the building that greeted us looked fairly new from the outside, with freshly painted walls and a manicured garden at the entrance. But when we walked through the doors, it looked as though the hotel was in the process of being renovated, and the outside was clearly the bit that had been made up first. It still looked like a decent place, so we weren’t too worried, and the smell of new paint and the sight of workers installing lights made us feel special as the first group of people staying in this hotel.

All of us were looking forward to being in our rooms and the chance to shower and relax before training. It was only when I saw maintenance workers carrying still-sealed mattresses to the rooms that it occurred to me that we were being put up in a hotel that was not fully ready for guests. I was only half-right. Actually, it was not ready at all.

Recent findings suggest that when we got to our rooms, they were empty: no mattresses on the beds, no lightbulbs in the lamps and, worst of all, not a drop of water in the taps. This made us all a little worried, but we were told it would be sorted out as soon as we had finished our training. We did have lunch at the hotel, although by now I was suspicious of things and particularly of the spread of fish and chicken, and then left for training. At least that went smoothly, and we expected to get back to suitable accommodation. No such luck.

It has been revealed that we returned to beds being made but still had no lights or running water. After a training session in extremely warm conditions, we were all dripping with sweat from head to toe and we had to make another proposal. A few of our players spotted a river just outside the hotel and said they were going to go there to rinse themselves off. I thought they were joking.

Sources indicate that when I looked again, the players had stripped down to their tights and sports bras, wrapped themselves in their pristine white hotel towels with their toiletries in hand and were heading out the door. If I wanted to be clean, I realised, I had to join them. My hesitation was twofold: I had never washed in a river before and wasn’t sure whether it was hygienic, but I was also still quite young and didn’t want to expose my body in public. I had to get over my qualms quite quickly. Fortunately, we didn’t have to wash in the river again. No one knows how, but when we opened the taps the following day, the water gushed out.

According to recent reports, with that kind of preparation, and Nigeria being as strong a team as they were, it was hardly a surprise that we lost 2-0. We experienced Nigeria’s off the field tactics first-hand. I did have one happy memory from the match, though. The Nigerian centre-back, Onome Ebi, who would go on to become the first African to play in six World Cups between 2003 and 2023, gave me her jersey. We both wore No 5 and she was the first international to give me her shirt. Given how much my Banyana Banyana jersey meant to me, I understood how special and symbolic this moment was, and I have stored it in my memory to this day.

This is an edited extract from 185: The Janine van Wyk Story is published by Karavan Press and available on Amazon in the United Kingdom.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

In a recent development, following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

Sources indicate that but here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that but that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the newly introduced debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

This development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

Recent findings suggest that to understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social problems, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, for 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding fresh investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary.".

Recent findings suggest that the rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

Nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are prepares for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, people born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

Industry observers note that the pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that but the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

Industry observers note that the key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

Industry observers note that at the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

It has been revealed that this would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This also means that interest rates on upcoming loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year.".

Sports memorabilia platform MatchWornShirt has secured upcoming backing from a group of active and former footballers, alongside North American sports investors.

Announced on Tuesday, the funding round is led by Gamma Waves Partners, a global sports and technology investment platform founded by former Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini, Andrea Agnelli and Rocco Benetton.

In a recent development, former Chelsea and England captain John Terry and current Tottenham Hotspur defender Tosin Adarabioyo have invested individually. Premier League brothers Jurrien Timber (Arsenal), and Quinten Timber (Crystal Palace), have also joined the round through Joyned Capital, a private investment club for professional athletes.

Outside football, the investment group includes basketball player Kevin Durant and Rich Kleiman’s 35V, along with the ownership group behind the NBA's Indiana Pacers and WNBA's Indiana Fever.

The capital injection follows a year in which MWS expanded its physical presence in North America ahead of the 2026 World Cup and agreed inaugural partnerships in the NBA, WNBA, NFL and NHL.

MWS were founded in Amsterdam in 2017 by brothers Tijmen and Bob Zonderwijk, the idea initially coming about during a search for an Ajax shirt for their father.

The organization now partners with more than 450 clubs worldwide to auction authentic, game-worn items.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I first got involved in match-worn shirts by selling them for charity, seeing the unique emotional value these items hold for fans,” Chiellini stated. “Today, it is exciting to see the category evolve, as collectors increasingly recognise the significance and value of these pieces of sporting history.

It has been revealed that “MatchWornShirt is building the infrastructure to connect fans and collectors with authentic moments from sport, while helping sports organisations unlock newly introduced value from their intellectual property. We are excited to support the company's next phase of growth.”.

MWS co-founder and CEO Tijmen Zonderwijk noted the incoming shareholders align with the platform’s long-term strategy.

“The scale of the names and businesses involved in this group of investors demonstrates a collective passion for what we have already built here at MWS, and for that, we're incredibly proud,” he remarked.

“It also represents a shared vision for the future, and we're excited to accelerate the growth of the business whilst remaining true to our values.”.

The individual size of Terry and co's investment has not been disclosed at this time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that although the millions of gamers who are pulling sickies would beg to differ, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI wasn’t the most exciting midnight launch involving a sprawling enterprise full of shady characters. Over in Zurich, the clock also struck 12 on the candidate deadline for next year’s Fifa presidential election, leaving those of us who have no interest in video games with our own chaotic, multi-billion-dollar sandbox where untouchable bosses bend the rules to suit themselves. While online carjackers are busy exploring a “most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world”, football’s real-life power brokers are gearing up for a March showdown in the actual city of Rabat.

For years, Gianni Infantino has looked nailed-on to glide into a fourth term of office completely unopposed, but following his disastrous Fifa Forward Enterprise wheeze to flog stakes in the World Cup to his American pals on the cheap, many of the emperor’s former allies have finally turned against him. In the wake of the revolt, European national associations withdrew their backing for Infantino and, on Thursday morning, Fifa confirmed the 56-year-old will face his first contested election since parking his backside on the throne a decade ago. Sadly for all those who would like nothing more than to see him deposed, Infantino remains the red-hot favourite in what will be a three-horse race.

Sources indicate that leading the charge for the mutineers is Philippe Diallo, the 63-year-old French Football Federation president who was unanimously anointed as Europe’s preferred candidate after their actual preferred candidate, Arsène Wenger, decided not to throw his chapeau in the ring. His billing by Uefa’s vice-president, Laura McAllister, as a man “who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform” at Fifa conveniently overlooks the fact that, as recently as five months ago, Diallo’s own federation signed a letter formally endorsing Infantino again. Joining Diallo in the battle to prise Gianni’s fingers off the levers of power is Kozo Tashima, the 68-year-old honorary president of the Japan FA. He could yet stand aside to avoid a split of the vote from Fifa’s 211 members who want Infantino booted to the door marked “Do One!”. Unfortunately, Ramon Vega, the former Switzerland and Tottenham defender, won’t be on the ballot. He had again unveiled his candidacy but proved unable to scare up the five member-association endorsements required.

In a recent development, between now and Fifa’s March congress, all three candidates must pass a Fifa eligibility and integrity check, a feat which shouldn’t be beyond the two pretenders, given Infantino has repeatedly come through it with flying colours while helping to overhaul the committees tasked with marking his papers along the way. Assuming he once again clears the hurdle of being vetted by his own organisation, the next four months promise a familiar blur of private jets, palm-greasing and disingenuous crawling. While a generation of gamers will spend winter pulling off virtual heists in Vice City, when it comes to bending the rules in your favour, nobody plays the game quite like the Fifa final boss.

Talks have started over Manchester City star Josko Gvardiol's exit from the Etihad.

That's according to one report, which claims that the Croatian defender's departure may have begun as early as the summer, with the future of the Citizens uncertain and a potential points deduction coming after an independent commission found the club guilty of over a hundred charges of financial rule-breaking.

Manchester City have launched an appeal – but an exodus could well be on the way, with Gvardiol the first domino.

January isn't the optimal time for transfer business, but Barcelona have interest in Gvardiol, as per AS via Sport Witness, with Hansi Flick wanting to improve his defence if he's to land a sixth Champions League title in Catalonia this season.

The report states that the Blaugrana asked about taking the 24-year-old along with Rodri while negotiating a move for the 2024 Ballon d'Or winner – but that the deal is “almost impossible” this winter due to the La Liga champions needing to raise funds to secure a major new signing.

That's where Manchester United come into play, with the Red Devils languishing in the relegation zone and having just hired Mauricio Pochettino to turn fortunes around.

United have an interest in Alejandro Balde, with the La Masia graduate failing to get the requisite playing time under Flick, and should Pochettino request a fresh full-back, the signing could well bolster the coffers for Barça to pursue Gvardiol.

Gvardiol is mentioned to be wanted by Flick for his athleticism and his ability to play both centrally and at left-back, but having signed a new deal at the Etihad Stadium over the summer, he may be completely unattainable now.

City maintain their innocence over the 115 charges, but should the club face a serious penalty, Gvardiol would surely reconsider his future, despite his recent contract extension.

The Athletic have noted that RB Leipzig’s Castello Lukeba is an option for Barcelona – as is United's own Lisandro Martinez, who fell out with club hierarchy recently over comments aimed at his team's recruitment over the summer.

The same report also mentions that United made a “deadline day check” on Balde but decided not to go any further with the deal.

Gvardiol is worth €75 million, according to Transfermarkt. City face Fulham when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

  • Seven successive Premier League wins to start his City reign, a record for a fresh manager in the competition, breaking one jointly-held by Guardiola, gave the impression that this might be a smooth passing of the torch after all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 14:40 EST, 20 November 2026.

In a recent development, diet Pep is losing his fizz. Enzo Maresca may look like Pep Guardiola, may have learned his craft under his Manchester City predecessor, but his quest to follow in his mentor’s footsteps has all gone a bit flat.

Seven successive Premier League wins to start his City reign, a record for a fresh manager in the competition, breaking one jointly-held by Guardiola, gave the impression that this might be a smooth passing of the torch after all.

Three months in, and three defeats on the spin that left them six points behind Arsenal have made it clear that something is not clicking for Maresca.

Sources indicate that is the uncertainty around the potential punishment following that guilty verdict taking its toll? Is Maresca just suffering from his usual late autumn dips? He suffered similar tricky periods around late October and early November at Leicester and his first season at Chelsea too.

Or is there something at the heart of his side, of his system, that’s finally being exposed?

Enzo Maresca's Man City have slumped to three straight Premier League defeats after a promising start to the season.

It has been revealed that guardiola’s City was all about control. Keep the ball, dominate the pitch, play the game at your pace, on your terms.

Maresca’s City, regardless of how well they started the season, has been about anything but. It has been about triumph amid chaos, about moments of magic more than the overarching method.

Without that control, City’s defensive challenges have been laid bare. The 13 goals they have let in after 10 games is their most at this stage since 2008. They haven’t kept a clean sheet in their last eight matches in all competitions. That's a drought longer than at any point under Guardiola.

Their biggest problem over City's three successive Premier League defeats is just how susceptible they have been to counter attacks.

Only Newcastle have faced more shots this season following ‘fast breaks’ – data giants Opta's term for counter attacks – than City’s 17, and 11 of those have come in the last three games: six against Nottingham Forest, two of which led to goals, three against Brighton and another two against Aston Villa.

Maresca’s side are being more profligate in possession, too. Over the first seven games of the season, they lost the ball 120 times a game on average – one of the best figures in the division. Since then, it’s closer to 140.

City have been wasteful in possession and regularly overrun on the counter, with Elliot Anderson (centre) too often left isolated in midfield.

ANDERSON CAN'T DO IT ALL ON HIS OWN.

In a recent development, many of these problems have their roots in Maresca's serious problems in midfield. Rodri, the best holding midfielder of his generation, was always going to be hard to replace but Maresca appears to be expecting Elliot Anderson to do it all on his own.

In a recent development, anderson is at his best when he’s free to get up and down the pitch, box to box, using his physicality not just in winning the ball back but progressing it. No midfielder played more passes into the final third last season than Anderson at Forest. At one stage of the campaign, he had played more progressive passes than any other player across Europe’s top five leagues.

And yet Maresca is forcing Anderson to play as the sitter while his golden boy Enzo Fernandez, whom he pushed City to sign in the summer for £125million, is roaming free and high up the pitch.

Maresca likes his teams to build up in a 3-1-6 shape, which sees Fernandez push up as an extra attacking midfielder, and leaves Anderson manning the fort alone.

When City lose the ball, though, it leaves them wide open.

Sources indicate that this is the opening goal City conceded against Forest. Josko Gvardiol wants to play the ball inside but has only red shirts and empty green space ahead of him. Anderson is the only man free, but even he is too high and has a Forest player ready to cut off the pass. Eventually, Gvardiol gets robbed and Forest score.

According to recent reports, A lack of options for Josko Gvardiol (left) led to Forest's opener against City. Enzo Fernandez (circled) was caught high up the pitch, way ahead of the deeper Anderson (also circled).

Here’s another moment in the defeat by Brighton.

It has been revealed that the Seagulls break forward on the flank and Anderson races over to close the ball down. Fernandez is, you guessed it, high up the pitch.

City have no midfield cover to stop the ball inside, Abdukodir Khusanov gets drawn in and leaves loads of space in behind for Yasin Ayari to exploit and cross to Maxim De Cuyper for a great chance.

The lack of protection offered by Anderson and especially the more advanced Fernandez was again on show against Brighton, who were able to exploit the acres of space left in midfield.

Industry observers note that fernandez is doing what Maresca wants, but it’s not working. Maresca needs more from him, especially when Anderson’s instincts are to press and harass and bully, which can leave gaps when he does not yet read the game as comprehensively as Rodri.

Sources indicate that anderson sits in the top five for ball recoveries among midfielders to have played 500 minutes this season. Fernandez is in the bottom five. That figure becomes even more alarming when you consider Anderson has created more chances from open play than Fernandez, too.

Ayyoub Bouaddi demonstrated at the World Cup that he had the most similar profile to Rodri. It might be time for Maresca to put some faith in him.

According to recent reports, maresca has always wanted his goalkeeper to be an 11th outfielder. In his one season at Leicester, Mads Hermansen played more passes than any goalkeeper in Championship history. During his time at Chelsea, there was a shaky moment in a draw with Arsenal when loud groans greeted a misplaced pass from Robert Sanchez.

‘I am the guy who asks Robert to do that,’ mentioned Maresca after that game. ‘The moment he stops doing that, he is not going to play.’.

Donnarumma, though, for all his (usually) excellent shot-stopping, is anything but a ball-playing goalkeeper. The ball rolled under his foot from a simple back pass against Coventry and so nearly crept over the line. He gifted France an early lead while on international duty with Italy when he passed the ball straight to Michael Olise.

Only two keepers made more errors leading to shots than Donnarumma across the course of last season, with many of those being with his feet, like when he gifted Kai Havertz an equaliser in City's victory over Arsenal in April.

Gianluigi Donnarumma has never been good with his feet - now his excellent shot-stopping has taken a dip too.

The Italian should have easily dealt with Nicolas Jackson's second goal in City's 2-1 loss at Aston Villa.

The decision to let James Trafford leave in the summer, especially with Guardiola’s impending departure and a manager like Maresca coming in, is looking ever more misguided.

Sources indicate that trafford is not immune to mistakes either, of course. He erred badly when trying to play out from the back for City against Spurs last season and made an almost identical howler for Leeds at Bournemouth in October. But he is still far more confident at playing out from the back than Donnarumma.

The double blow for Maresca is that the trade-off with Donnarumma – where he makes up for his weakness with the ball at his feet by making saves that other keepers can’t make – is no longer paying off either.

Nicolas Jackson’s shot squirmed straight through him to hand Villa victory and condemn City to their first defeat of the season.

When you are coughing up chances as frequently as City are, Maresca needs his keeper to be on top form.

According to recent reports, do you know who is keeping the ball out of his net? James Trafford. He boasts the highest save percentage of any goalkeeper in the top flight, keeping out 81 per cent of the shots on target coming his way. Donnarumma is 15th, on less than 66 per cent.

Industry observers note that according to Opta’s expected data, Trafford has also prevented more than four goals that he should have conceded from the quality of the shots he’s faced. Again, he’s the best in the Premier League. Donnarumma is middle of the pack.

‘At the moment, I’m not thinking about the goalkeeping situation,’ mentioned Maresca recently. Without Trafford there and just 34-year-old Geronimo Rulli as back-up, he doesn’t really have a choice but to persist with Donnarumma and hope he improves.

When the goals stop flowing for Erling Haaland, City can't mask all their other problems.

So used are we now to seeing the Norwegian on the scoresheet, having notched nine in City’s opening eight matches, that when he goes just two games without a goal it feels as if he’s on a barren spell.

The issue, though, is less down to Haaland and more that City’s build-up in recent weeks is struggling to get him into the game.

Recent findings suggest that city are finding it more difficult to get Haaland on the ball. His touches per game are falling steadily but, crucially, so are the quality of the chances his team-mates are creating for him.

According to recent reports, haaland had more than one Opta-defined 'significant chance' in five of City’s opening seven games. He’s had just one come his way in each of their three defeats.

According to recent reports, his expected goals (xG) tally is dropping too. Across City’s winning streak, Haaland’s average xG per match was 0.81. Only once, against Liverpool, did it drop below 0.5.

Over the three defeats, it’s just 0.45 and has not once gone above 0.5.

Antoine Semenyo missing the last three games through injury has not helped, especially when teams now try to pack the middle of the pitch and force City wide.

Haaland will come good, he always does, but City need to start serving him again if Maresca wants to get through this tricky spell and stop the vultures from circling.

‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience.
  • Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria.
  • It has been revealed that four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience.

Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” claims the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.”.

It has been revealed that four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to a BigShoe initiative.

Recent findings suggest that “They told me he was going to receive the award, but he didn’t know, so they asked whether I could get a letter from one of the children we had helped,” Fiesser says. “I was really proud of Bukayo, I think the way he did it was really special. He stood there so strongly for all these children around the world that nobody sees and nobody hears. He gave them a voice. He took the attention away from himself and put it into action. That’s how I know Bukayo. It’s never about him, it’s always about the people we help. He’s incredible.”.

Saka, who donated more than 1,000 school uniforms to children in his home borough of Ealing in west London last year to help with the cost of living crisis, is understood to have heard about BigShoe from Antonio Rüdiger after the Real Madrid and Germany defender told him about some of the work he had done with the organisation, including in Sierra Leone.

It has been revealed that bigShoe has also worked with Philipp Lahm and Mesut Özil. Fiesser states Saka and his family have taken a particularly close interest in projects he supports.

Recent findings suggest that “When we had 150 life-changing surgeries taking place in Nigeria, he would message me asking to see pictures,” she claims. “He wanted to know what was happening and whether everybody was safe. He always asks whether the team has returned safely. I don’t know how he manages to find the time, but he does.

Industry observers note that “His family are very similar. They genuinely want to make a big impact and provide meaningful help. I wouldn’t describe Bukayo as simply a donor to BigShoe. He’s more like a member of the BigShoe team. I know that he stands behind us.”.

Industry observers note that bigShoe was established by four friends in Germany after the 2006 World Cup. As part of its latest projects in Rwanda and Nigeria, about 3,000 people had eye examinations and were given glasses if required. “Giving a child a pair of glasses can change their life,” Fiesser states. “We also help entire families. If a father can’t see properly, he might not be able to work or read. That affects the whole family.”.

It has been revealed that bigShoe recently renovated a school in Rwanda and provided clean drinking water through a filtration system. It has also built a library and provided private changing facilities for girls. “Once a month, some girls miss school because they don’t have suitable facilities or somewhere private to change,” claims Fiesser. “We built facilities so they can continue attending school and have a quiet, private area.”.

Saka’s hectic playing schedule means he has yet to make a visit, but his family have been on the ground in Rwanda and he was heavily involved in funding earthquake relief projects in Morocco and Turkey. “We provided container homes for people affected by the earthquakes,” says Fiesser. “I knew I could count on him. It’s always important to Bukayo that we make a big impact. He doesn’t want money to be wasted. When I present a project to him, he wants to understand it properly. He needs to know exactly what we’re doing before he makes a decision. He’s a 100% person. Whatever he does, he gives it everything.”.

According to recent reports, saka’s mother, Adenike, is believed to be a driving force behind her son’s charitable work. Fiesser describes her as “one of the most amazing women I’ve met”. Plans are being made for the next projects, which include providing health insurance to families in Nigeria and food packages for children in Rwanda over Christmas, even if Saka has typically been pushing for something more long-term.

“He doesn’t just want to give someone food,” Fiesser states. “Of course, food is vital, and we’re providing that too, but he wants to change lives. You can help someone, but if the help doesn’t last, then it hasn’t achieved what you really wanted. If we all work together, it doesn’t matter which team we’re supporting or which country we’re helping. We’re all part of one world.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Undergraduate students on university campuses played a massive part in spreading viral variants during the COVID-19 pandemic.Credit: Leonard Ortiz/Digital First Media/Orange County Register/Getty.

Universities have become hotbeds of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, according to a massive analysis of more than 85,000 viral genome sequences and other data collected from people with COVID-19.

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you.

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you.

Industry observers note that the study, published on 19 November in the journal Cell1, finds that viral transmission between 2021 and 2023 was highest among adolescents aged 15 to 18 in schools, undergraduates at university, and residents in nursing facilities. Undergraduates, in particular, were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging genetic variants of SARS-CoV-2.

Surprisingly, however, staff members at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. So, for example, professors were about as likely to get COVID-19 from the coffee baristas in their university towns as they were to get it from a student at their university.

It has been revealed that the analysis is among the largest to bring together viral genomic sequences with medical data from people with COVID-19. “The scale is truly impressive,” says Bill Hanage, who studies the evolution of infectious diseases at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, Massachusetts. “It’s an example of the depth and the detail of the picture that can be painted using the medium of population genomics.”.

The findings were based on data collected from COVID-19 tests taken by people in Massachusetts, between November 2021 and January 2023. The genomic data allowed researchers to trace the path of SARS-CoV-2 variants that emerged over time, and to link this with epidemiological data about the study participants, such as their age and whether they had been vaccinated against COVID-19.

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

Overall, the team found that booster vaccinations helped to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. This was true even for BA.1, an Omicron variant that started to circulate in Massachusetts in late 2021 — a striking result because COVID-19 vaccines at that time hadn’t yet been updated to protect against BA.1, Hanage notes. “That’s an important illustration of how vaccines, even when they’re not perfect, can still be beneficial,” he says.
